source.title: Do Vision and Language Models Share Concepts? A Vector Space Alignment Study
source.authors: Jiaang Li; Yova Kementchedjhieva; Constanza Fierro; Anders Søgaard

record.tranche_reason: Tests cross-modal representational alignment and its scaling using Procrustes mapping and held-out retrieval precision, rather than the original study’s measurement recipe.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own cross-modal alignment results. Cited findings from other work are not included as rows. Many model-by-model values are shown only in figures and are not extracted individually. The study uses image classes and aliases or words, not ordinary image-caption pairs.
record.test_reason: Measures whether vision and language model representations align, and how that changes with model size. It uses supervised orthogonal Procrustes maps and held-out P@k retrieval over 14 vision models and 14 language models, not the original's mutual-kNN recipe. It is not one of the original sources.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, but incomplete. The authors conclude that LM and vision-model geometries are surprisingly similar, that LMs partially converge toward vision geometry subject to dispersion, polysemy and frequency, and that similarity grows with model size (log-linear, no saturation). They argue that because the world is the only common source, this suggests internal world models and challenges Bender and Koller. They concede that mapping currently requires supervision.
record.recipe_differences: Uses supervised orthogonal Procrustes mapping and held-out P@k retrieval between image and language concept representations; tests a cross-modal setting rather than the original Platonic study’s broader representation comparisons.
record.method_sensitivity: Alignment precision varies with image dispersion, language dispersion, alias polysemy, alias frequency, parts of speech, and training-dictionary size. The study reports P@1, P@10, and P@100, but does not compare alternative representation-similarity measures.
record.peer_reviewed: Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The mapping is supervised and depends on paired examples; the main evaluation is retrieval precision rather than a direct comparison of distance matrices. ImageNet-derived evaluation is noun-heavy, and input properties substantially affect precision. Five random splits are averaged, but no uncertainty estimates are reported. Several model-size results appear only in figures.
record.rows_left_out: Individual model-pair points in Figures 4, 6, 7, 9, and 10, and additional values in Tables 4–6, are not separately extracted; the aggregate scaling trend and representative condition-dependent table results are retained. Table 2 baseline entries are not split into separate rows because the flattened excerpt does not reliably associate every numeric entry with its baseline.

untested.parts: Capability or performance as the scaling axis (only parameter count is varied); within-modality convergence across architectures; objectives other than the listed families.
Full image-caption pairs (uses concept aliases and words); task performance of either model.
Entire version: no same-architecture, different-seed comparisons.
Stitching, relative representations and non-linear maps.
Entire version: no neurons, SAE features or circuits.
Alternative similarity measures (e.g., CKA, mutual kNN); only the P@k retrieval cutoff and input subsets vary.
Whether shared data or objectives, rather than a common world model, cause the alignment. Not experimentally isolated; the authors only argue the world is the sole common source.

missing.what: CLIP vision encoders, trained with text, align better with LMs than pure vision models (e.g., P@100 94.1% mixed POS for CLIP-ViT-L with OPT30B). Shared training signal raises alignment, which bears on V7's other-causes clause; vision scaling is again marginal.
P@1 and P@10 for ResNet152–OPT30B (about 1/20 and 1/3 versus 64.1% at P@100). Shows the result depends strongly on the retrieval cutoff k.
Failure of unsupervised (unpaired) mapping algorithms, with partial recovery only from a noised supervised initialization.
Image-dispersion results for SegFormer-B5 are mixed (60.6/60.4/57.6), unlike ResNet and MAE. MAE-Huge and SegFormer rows for the other bins are also not extracted.
Ranking of vision families: ResNet > SegFormer > MAE. Even the fully self-supervised MAE aligns far above baseline (e.g., 56.7 in the low image-dispersion bin with OPT30B).

record.verdict_notes: Several record links were too broad. Input-subset rows were linked to V2 and V6 at once; I split them, with reference bins on V2 and weaker bins on V6. R3 (a single model pair) was linked to V1, and R2 to V7; both removed. Alignment is measured as supervised retrieval precision, not a kernel or similarity metric, so comparisons with Huh et al. need care.

versions.untested_parts: The study measures model size, not task capability or performance; it does not establish convergence across every combination of architecture, objective, data, and modality.
The paired language items are concepts, aliases, and words rather than full captions; the study does not directly measure both models’ general task performance.
No same-architecture comparisons across random initializations, shared features, or subspaces.
Tests supervised linear Procrustes mappings only; no stitching, relative representations, or successful mapping without paired supervision.
No recurring interpretable features, neurons, SAE features, or circuits are measured.
Tests sensitivity to input properties and retrieval cutoffs, but not alternative representation-similarity measures or out-of-distribution inputs.
Reports incomplete alignment and weak gains from scaling vision models, but does not experimentally isolate shared training data or objectives as causes.
